credits.readme:
The leaves: *Wooden Writing Tablets*, Coptic, Byzantine Egypt, 500–700, wood
and wax, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 14.2.4a–d, Rogers Fund, 1914, CC0
(Open Access). Leaf b's written face, leaf d's two faces. Cut out, shadowed
and turned by `tools/cut-leaves.py`; nothing else in the photographs is
changed. The stylus is drawn after the Met's Cypriot bronze stylus
(74.51.5495, CC0), a reference only. Letterforms drawn for this component;
metrics font built with fontTools. Sounds synthesised in code. `tilt.js` and
`sound.js` are the shared Taste copies. No libraries at runtime.

`tools/` holds the small build scripts (Python, not needed at runtime):
`build-font.py` (the metrics font, needs fontTools), `cut-leaves.py` (the
leaves from the Met's photographs, needs Pillow, NumPy and SciPy) and
`make-sounds.py` (the two event sounds).

files.text:
correspondence

Leave a note

These are two leaves of a set of four, made in Egypt some time between 500 and 700 and now in the Metropolitan Museum. Each is a board of wood a hand and a half tall, hollowed to a shallow tray and filled with wax darkened with soot, so that a line scratched into it shows pale. The holes down one side took the cord that bound the set into a little book.

The left leaf still carries its last lesson, a Greek cursive in a quick hand, one line struck through with a single long stroke. The right leaf was levelled and left blank. Write on it with the keys: a bronze point ploughs each letter, and Backspace turns the stylus over so its flat end smooths the wax again.

A tablet was never new for long. Wax is levelled with the flat of the stylus or warmed and smoothed, and a pupil writes again. But a hard hand goes through the wax into the wood, and the wood keeps it. Most surviving Roman tablets, at Vindolanda and in the London Walbrook, have lost their wax entirely and are read from those scratches alone, several texts crossing one another.

This leaf has been used before. Hold it to the light: under the line in the wax are the alphabet and a maxim a child copied out and rubbed away.

# cera-tablet A text field that is a real wax tablet: two leaves of a Coptic set from Egypt, made between 500 and 700 and photographed by the Metropolitan Museum. The left leaf still carries its own Greek lesson, scratched in a quick cursive. The right leaf is smooth, and it is your field. Type, and a bronze stylus ploughs each letter into the wax as a single fine stroke: the point goes in blunt, drags round its corners and lifts away to a hairline, and the cut shows pale because it lifts the dark skin of the wax, with one side in shade from the lamp. Backspace, and the stylus turns over and its flat end drags the letters smooth. Write fast and hard and the point goes through the wax into the wood, and those scores outlast the smoothing: the deleted words linger faintly under the levelled wax. That is how most surviving Roman stylus tablets are read: the wax is long gone, and what is left are the scratches the point made in the wood. ```html
